title: Hearing before reading
hook: the Qur'an is first recited, heard, memorized, and only then read

segments.voice: Yesterday: taharah opened camp three's one whole day, five returns and everything leaning toward them. Your line was a day that bows. Day one hundred fifty-seven, and a new camp.

Nobody reads the lyrics of a lullaby. A child hears it in the dark, again and again, until one night the child sings it back. The words arrive through the ear. A mosque classroom on a Saturday morning works the same way: rows of kids, some rocking gently, repeating after a teacher, line by line, until the sound is in them. Some can recite whole surahs before they can read the script. This camp is about the text itself, and it starts where the text started: in the ear.
screen: `A SONG YOU NEVER READ.` → `KIDS REPEATING, LINE BY LINE.` → `THE TEXT STARTS IN THE EAR.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Muslim scholars connect the word Qur'an to a root meaning to read aloud, to recite: the Qur'an is the recitation. And tradition says the first word revealed, in a cave outside Mecca, was a command from that same root: iqra'. In Pickthall's translation, Surah al-Alaq opens: Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth. The Prophet ﷺ, Muslims say, could not read or write. So the Qur'an didn't arrive as a book. It arrived as sound, through the angel Jibril, a little at a time, over many years. The Prophet recited it; the companions heard and memorized it; some wrote it on whatever they had, palm stalks and thin flat stones. Bukhari reports that every Ramadan, Jibril went over all that had been revealed with him, aloud. Only after the Prophet's death was it gathered into a single written volume. The word for this reciting is tilawah. Arabic dictionaries give its root the sense of following, one thing after another, the way words follow words. And scholars point out a second meaning: to follow a text is also to live by it. To this day, the Qur'an is taught mouth to ear, teacher to student, in chains going back generation by generation. There are rules for how each letter is sounded, called tajwid. And a report in Abu Dawud says: beautify the Qur'an with your voices. The first listeners met it with their ears, not their eyes. For the next weeks, this camp walks through the thirtieth part, the last section, full of short surahs.
screen: `QUR'AN — THE RECITATION.` · `IQRA' — READ, RECITE.` · `SOUND FIRST, BOOK LATER.` · `TILAWAH — TO FOLLOW.` · then, large: `BEAUTIFY IT WITH YOUR VOICES.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and listen to the sounds already around you, the way you'd listen to music in a language you don't know yet: the rise and fall, the long vowels, the pauses. That's the ear a short surah asks for, al-Fatiha, al-Ikhlas or any of the last ones, heard from a reciter you like, without reading along or reaching for a translation yet.
Tilawah. Reciting the Qur'an aloud, from a root meaning to follow: word after word, and then in how you live. Today's word.
Your line: hear it first. The sound arrives first, and the meaning follows. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: Why do kids at the mosque learn to recite before they can read Arabic?
options: The Qur'an began as sound, recited aloud, and it's still taught mouth to ear.
Reading Arabic isn't allowed until a child has memorized the whole Qur'an.
Reciting is just practice; the real Qur'an is the book, read silently.
chat.meaning: The Qur'an arrived as sound, through Jibril, and is still taught teacher to student. Its very name means the recitation.
